body:
FWIW, while this is a legitimate bug, this seems like a very odd use of serialize. Why not just write it as:

``` ruby
class Category < ActiveRecord::Base
  def match_regexp
    Regexp.new(super)
  end
end
```

@sgrif That's a fair comment.  The simple answer is that I didn't write it that way.  :)

My first thought was to serialize the Regexp in the database, so that's how I wrote it.  But as you note, there are some simple changes I can make to get this working in Rails 4.2.0.

:)

Either way I'll look into the regression.

Can you provide an executable test case using [this template](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/master/guides/bug_report_templates/active_record_master.rb) that passes on 4.1? I get the same errors on 4.1.

@sgrif Sure.  Added here - https://github.com/petergoldstein/regexp_issue_testapp/blob/master/test_script/bug_report.rb .  I've confirmed that the script runs successfully with Rails 4.1, fails with Rails 4.2.

I think the key issue is that in my code I always set the value of the Regexp attribute before saving.  I suspect that 4.1 would error out if you tried to save an ActiveRecord with a nil attribute for serialize.  But 4.2 does some default value checking on the attribute on object creation, meaning that a non-nil default value is required in the database.

I see. I'm less inclined to see this as a bug then, as it's definitely not a case that we really "supported" before. Reading an attribute in a supported case should never result in an error. I do think that we can produce a better error message when you originally call `serialize`, though.
@sgrif That's reasonable, although I'm still not sure why a serialized attribute can't be nil from a framework design perspective.

@petergoldstein Basically, the original idea was that you usually wanted an empty array or an empty hash, and so `serialize :foo, Array` was just shorthand for setting the default. I agree with you that it was a questionable design decision. It's pretty painful to change at this point, though. We're shying away from `serialize`. Most examples will probable use https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/master/activerecord/lib/active_record/attributes.rb instead once that's made public in Rails 5.

In your case, the simplest fix would be to just not pass a class to `serialize`, since it's optional.
@sgrif I've already modified my code per your original suggestion, so I don't have a lot of skin in the game at this point.  Happy to defer to your judgement on this issue.
